analysis.one_liner: Quadruples the federal excise tax on corporate stock buybacks from 1% to 4%.
analysis.headline: The bill to quadruple the tax on stock buybacks never got a hearing or a vote in the Senate Finance Committee and died when the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: Corporations spend billions of dollars buying back their own stock, which pushes share prices up and rewards large shareholders and executives. A 1% federal tax on those buybacks already exists; this bill would have raised it to 4%. The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: The general public, in two ways: the tax raises federal revenue from large corporations and wealthy shareholders rather than from wage earners, and a higher tax modestly discourages companies from pouring cash into buybacks instead of wages, investment, or hiring. The Congressional Research Service summary describes it purely as a rate increase on repurchases of corporate stock.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the excise tax on corporate stock repurchases from 1% to 4%, applying to buybacks after enactment.
Adds an adjustment so companies do not get a buyback tax break for stock issued to highly paid 'covered employees', closing a route around the tax tied to executive compensation.
The new rate applies immediately after enactment, so companies could not front-run it by scheduling buybacks in advance.

analysis.who_pays: Large publicly traded companies that buy back their own stock and their biggest shareholders, including executives whose compensation is tied to share price. Some of the cost could reach ordinary workers indirectly, since many own stock through retirement funds, and some economists argue the tax mostly shifts corporate payout practices rather than raising much revenue.

drawbacks.text: A buyback excise tax is a blunt tool: it taxes a transaction rather than wealth or income, and companies can respond by shifting to dividends or debt, so the burden can land partly on retirement savers and other regular shareholders rather than only on the wealthy.

The bill sets the rate and effective date but offers no analysis in the record of how much revenue it would raise or how strongly a 4% rate would actually change corporate behavior; a modest rate increase may simply be absorbed by large firms.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gain to ordinary people is real but modest: a few percentage points of tax on a wealthy transaction, plus a small nudge against buybacks. The main honest objection is that the tax is easy for corporations to design around and that some of its cost could leak to ordinary retirement investors. It is a fair, if incremental, step rather than a sweeping fix.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the Senate Finance Committee from the day it was introduced, with no hearing, no markup, and no vote, until the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sherrod Brown introduced the Stock Buyback Accountability Act on February 14, 2023, joined by six original cosponsors including Ron Wyden, the chair of the Finance Committee to which the bill was referred.
The bill would raise the excise tax on corporate stock repurchases from 1% to 4% under Internal Revenue Code section 4501.
It also adjusts the tax so that stock issued to highly paid 'covered employees' is excluded from the repurchase calculation, closing a carve-out tied to executive compensation.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance on the day of introduction, and no further action of any kind appears in the record for the rest of the 118th Congress.
Ten Senate Democrats (the sponsor plus 9 cosponsors) supported the bill; no Republican sponsored or cosponsored it, and the bill never advanced past committee referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large public companies and their biggest shareholders are better off, because the 4% buyback tax never became law and buybacks remained taxed at only 1%. Committee members of both parties who preferred not to force a vote also kept the issue off the floor.

for.name: Sherrod Brown
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited nine Democratic cosponsors.

for.name: Ron Wyden
for.what_they_did: Signed on as an original cosponsor at introduction.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill after its referral; it received no action for nearly two years.

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: None sponsored or cosponsored the bill, leaving it without any Republican support that might have pressed committee action.

sides.party_line_note: All ten supporters were Democrats and no Republican sponsored or cosponsored the bill; the caucus-level split meant the bill had no path past a committee controlled by members unwilling to move it.

industries.industry: Large publicly traded corporations and major shareholders
industries.note: The bill would have quadrupled their tax on buybacks from 1% to 4% and closed an adjustment tied to stock issued to highly paid employees. Its death leaves the 1% rate in place, preserving buybacks as a favored, lightly taxed way to return cash to big shareholders and executives.

Ordinary workers holding index funds or 401(k)s would indirectly bear part of the tax through fund-level buybacks, but the same people pay the taxes that fund the government and bear the cost of forgone wages when firms prefer buybacks to investment.
